metadata.title: A Short Proof of Bernoulli Disjointness via the Local Lemma

extraction_notes.note: Theorem 1.1 is attributed to GTWZ (origin external) but the paper's main contribution is a new proof of it; kept TP1 external and the prose proof PP1 (all of Section 2) as origin paper.

Both main proofs are prose without proof environments; PP1 spans the whole of Section 2 (including Lemma 2.3 and its proof, nested as a setup step), PP5 starts after the definition of $V_\varphi$ and runs to the end of Section 4.

The sentence deducing Theorem 3.4 from Alon-Spencer Cor. 5.1.2 plus compactness was split out of the surrounding remark as a sketch proof of the external LLL; could also be left as part of remark RP2.
The one-sentence attribution 'For Gamma = Z, Theorem 1.1 was proven earlier by Furstenberg' was kept as an external theorem specializing TP1; it could be read as a historical remark.

Abstract restatement of Theorem 1.1, the historical sentence on the constant 4 vs e in the LLL, the intro discussion of GTWZ's group-theoretic proof (separated covering property), and the acknowledgments get no nodes.

\label{lemma:rec}
		If $X$ is a minimal $\Gamma$-flow and $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set, then there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \Gamma$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \0$.

nodes.statement: Since X is minimal, the orbit of each point in X intersects U, and thus X = Gamma cdot U. The compactness of X implies that there is a finite subset T subset Gamma such that X = T cdot U. Say that a set L subseteq Gamma is emphdright T-separated if lambda_1T cap lambda_2T = \0 for every pair of distinct lambda_1, lambda_2 in L. Since T is finite while Gamma is infinite, there is an infinite right T-separated subset L subseteq Gamma. Consider any x in U. For each lambda in L, we have lambda^-1 cdot x in T cdot U, i.e., x in lambda T cdot U. In other words, for each lambda in L, there is tau_lambda in T with x in lambda tau_lambda cdot U. Since L is right T-separated, the set S coloneqq setlambda tau_lambda \,:\, lambda in L is infinite, and we are done.
nodes.raw_latex: Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \Gamma \cdot U$. The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \Gamma$ such that $X = T \cdot U$. Say that a set $L \subseteq \Gamma$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \0$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$. Since $T$ is finite while $\Gamma$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \Gamma$. Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$. Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \coloneqq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done.
nodes.clean_text: Since X is minimal, the orbit of each point in X intersects U, and thus X = Gamma cdot U. The compactness of X implies that there is a finite subset T subset Gamma such that X = T cdot U. Say that a set L subseteq Gamma is emphdright T-separated if lambda_1T cap lambda_2T = \0 for every pair of distinct lambda_1, lambda_2 in L. Since T is finite while Gamma is infinite, there is an infinite right T-separated subset L subseteq Gamma. Consider any x in U. For each lambda in L, we have lambda^-1 cdot x in T cdot U, i.e., x in lambda T cdot U. In other words, for each lambda in L, there is tau_lambda in T with x in lambda tau_lambda cdot U. Since L is right T-separated, the set S coloneqq setlambda tau_lambda \,:\, lambda in L is infinite, and we are done.

nodes.statement: First recall some basic facts about finite graphs. Let G be a finite graph with vertex set V and edge set E. A subset I subseteq V is emphdindependent epin G if no two vertices in I are adjacent to each other. A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of G has at most d neighbors, then V can be partitioned into d+1 independent sets. In particular, G has an independent set of size at least |V|/(d+1). Now let G be the graph with vertex set F in which distinct vertices sigma, sigma' in F are adjacent if and only if Dsigma cap Dsigma' neq \0, or, equivalently, sigma' in D^-1Dsigma. Every sigma in F has at most |D^-1D| - 1 leqslant |D|^2 - 1 neighbors in G epwe are subtracting 1 to account for the fact that sigma is not adjacent to itself. Therefore, G has an independent set L of size at least |F|/|D|^2, and that is precisely what we need.
nodes.raw_latex:
First recall some basic facts about finite graphs. Let $G$ be a finite graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. A subset $I \subseteq V$ is \emphd{independent \ep{in $G$}} if no two vertices in $I$ are adjacent to each other. A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of $G$ has at most $d$ neighbors, then $V$ can be partitioned into $d+1$ independent sets. In particular, $G$ has an independent set of size at least $|V|/(d+1)$.
		
		Now let $G$ be the graph with vertex set $F$ in which distinct vertices $\sigma$, $\sigma' \in F$ are adjacent if and only if $D\sigma \cap D\sigma' \neq \0$, or, equivalently, $\sigma' \in D^{-1}D\sigma$. Every $\sigma \in F$ has at most $|D^{-1}D| - 1 \leqslant |D|^2 - 1$ neighbors in $G$ \ep{we are subtracting $1$ to account for the fact that $\sigma$ is not adjacent to itself}. Therefore, $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size at least $|F|/|D|^2$, and that is precisely what we need.

A subset I subseteq V is emphdindependent epin G if no two vertices in I are adjacent to each other. A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of G has at most d neighbors, then V can be partitioned into d+1 independent sets. In particular, G has an independent set of size at least |V|/(d+1). Now let G be the graph with vertex set F in which distinct vertices sigma, sigma' in F are adjacent if and only if Dsigma cap Dsigma' neq \0, or, equivalently, sigma' in D^-1Dsigma. Every sigma in F has at most |D^-1D| - 1 leqslant |D|^2 - 1 neighbors in G epwe are subtracting 1 to account for the fact that sigma is not adjacent to itself. Therefore, G has an independent set L of size at least |F|/|D|^2, and that is precisely what we need.
